persona: Monetization-first audience strategist: I start from who has already paid money in this category and what exactly they paid for, then work backwards to the channel.
isolation: ran in parallel with A and B, no visibility of their output

language_market_position.reasoning: Chinese-language throughout, sequenced: mainland WeChat ecosystem first for the payment rail, then overseas Chinese diaspora for price tolerance - never English-first. The decisive fact is rails, not reach: a solo unincorporated founder CANNOT open a WeChat Pay merchant account (企业/个体工商户 + 营业执照 required), but CAN legally charge strangers today through 微信公众号付费阅读 (个人主体 allowed, ¥1-¥208 across 35 price tiers) or 小报童 (15% platform fee, no business license), with one-tap WeChat Pay conversion - while Stripe explicitly does not serve mainland-China-based users, making a USD-first launch rail-blocked until the founder entity/residence is confirmed. Against mainland: consumer willingness-to-pay for recipe content is demonstrably weak - 下厨房, the category leader in China, monetizes via 市集 commerce, B2B brand-sponsored recipes and paid classes, not consumer subscription. So the money is in the diaspora ($40/yr NYT Cooking, $50/yr Substack default are normal there) but the rail is in the mainland; the sequence resolves that, and Chinese-language content serves both. I reject (c) outright: English-language recipe content is the single most commoditized content market on the internet and the founder has no language edge, no distribution and no cost advantage there.
evidence: no evidence: could not retrieve any data on Chinese-diaspora willingness-to-pay for Chinese-language cooking content specifically - the weakest link in this recommendation

monetization_thesis.recommended_revenue_model: Paid seasonal content product on a recurring calendar - a 24-节气 market list + week of cooking annual pass sold as a 小报童 column / WeChat paid series. Not an app subscription, not ads, not affiliate. The product IS the calendar: the 节气 cycle gives 24 natural, pre-scheduled reasons to charge and re-engage, which is the only structural defence against the recipe category brutal churn.
monetization_thesis.price_point_hypothesis: China: ¥39 (~USD 5.5) for a single-season pack (6 节气, ~6 weeks of market lists + recipes); ¥128-¥199/yr (~USD 18-28) for the full 24-节气 annual pass. Diaspora/USD: USD 19 one-off Chinese Seasonal Pantry and Market Guide, USD 29-39/yr for the annual pass. Anchors: paid 小报童 columns commonly sit at ¥99; 公众号付费 tiers span ¥1-¥208; NYT Cooking is ~USD 5/mo or ~USD 40/yr; Paprika is a USD 4.99 mobile / USD 29.99 desktop one-off; Substack default is USD 5/mo or USD 50/yr.
monetization_thesis.fastest_path_to_first_dollar: Different from the long-run model, but only in packaging. Fastest: a ¥29-¥39 single-season 小报童 column, launched THIS month. 小报童 has no account-age gate and needs no business license; 微信公众号付费阅读 requires the account be 3+ months old with 3+ 原创 articles, so it cannot produce a first dollar inside 30 days. Concretely: publish 3-4 free 节气 市场食单 posts on 小红书, drive commenters to a personal WeChat, and sell the current-season pack at ¥39 with a ¥19 早鸟 code to the first 20. First dollar target: 14-21 days. The long-run model is the same content re-cut as a ¥128-¥199 annual pass plus, much later, B2B seasonal-produce sponsorship - but do not build for the annual pass before ten strangers have paid ¥39.
monetization_thesis.why_this_and_not_others: Not an app subscription: recipe content is infinitely free, and low-priced apps convert far worse than high-priced ones (RevenueCat 2025 report widely cited as ~9.8% median conversion for high-priced vs ~4.3% for low-priced apps - primary could not be fetched, flag as secondary), while the honest free-to-paid benchmark for content is a ~3% median, not the 5-10% platforms advertise. Not affiliate/grocery: Amazon Associates pays 1% on grocery/Amazon Fresh - an audience of a few thousand generates rounding-error revenue, and China has no equivalent nano-creator grocery rail. Not sponsorship: it requires reach the founder does not have, and reach is a banned metric here. Not B2B-to-farms: Western CSA software already ships a built-in recipe generator off the weekly harvest list, and farms pay only ~USD 80-200/mo for their entire software stack - a tiny ceiling, a long sales cycle, and no founder network into it.
evidence: no evidence: revenuecat.com is blocked from this environment - the high-price/low-price conversion split above is secondary reporting, not the primary, and must be re-verified before it drives any pricing decision

no evidence: no reliable public data found on churn for recipe/meal-planning subscriptions specifically; several search hits quoting 60% churn at 3 months trace to AI-generated content farms and should not be used

assumption_challenges: LOAD-BEARING: that the founder is resident in mainland China with no company. If they are actually resident overseas (or hold a HK/US/SG entity or a Stripe-eligible bank account), the rail constraint vanishes, the sequence inverts, and I would lead with the diaspora/USD product at USD 29-39/yr and treat mainland as the cheap content-testing ground.

LOAD-BEARING: that the primary interface language is Chinese. If shilingshipu.com is actually English-first, C1 and C2 are unbuildable as written and I would flip to (c) with a US CSA-member/farmers-market audience - but at materially lower confidence, because that is a crowded market with no founder edge.

LOAD-BEARING: that seasonal means 二十四节气 / Chinese market seasonality rather than a generic Western produce calendar. The 节气 frame is what makes the content culturally sticky, gives it 24 pre-scheduled paid moments a year, and makes it un-Googleable in a way a produce-calendar site is not. If the product is built on a generic Western produce calendar in Chinese, the differentiation collapses and I would score all three entry points ~0.2 lower.

That the founder can personally cook and photograph food to a credible standard. Recipe products convert on trust in the cook, not on database completeness. If the content is aggregated or AI-generated, no amount of channel work produces a paying cohort and I would recommend a tools/B2B pivot instead.
That the founder has a usable existing WeChat network. If the true starting point is zero WeChat contacts, the 私域 path adds 4-8 weeks before the first sale and C1 becomes the only viable opener.

That the site is hosted overseas. If it is hosted in mainland China without ICP备案 it can be taken down, killing the owned-asset leg of every entry point; if hosted overseas it loads slowly for mainland users and cannot integrate WeChat Pay - which is precisely why money routes through 小报童/公众号 rather than through the website.

entry_points.name: 菜市场食单 - Xiaohongshu seasonal market-list series
entry_points.target_audience: Chinese women 25-40 in tier-1/2 cities who cook 3+ times a week, already buy 养生/知识付费 products (¥29-¥199 columns, 知识星球 memberships), and shop at a wet market or on 叮咚/美团买菜. Willingness-to-pay signal: they already spend money on 养生 content and on 当季 ingredients - the spend exists, it is just not going to a recipe product yet.
entry_points.problem: Standing in the market or in front of the grocery app at 6pm with no idea what is actually in season, actually cheap, and actually worth cooking this week - and ending up buying the same five things and wasting a third of them.
entry_points.hook: 立秋这一周，我只买这5样菜：便宜、当季、不用再想吃什么
entry_points.content_format: 6-9 image 小红书 carousel per 节气 (cover = 节气 name + the 5 ingredients + a price; inner pages = one dish per ingredient, 3 steps each), plus an 800-character caption. Publish 2-3 per week, anchored to the real 节气 date.
entry_points.cta: 评论区回复「食单」，我把这一周的完整食单（含菜市场清单和预算）发你
entry_points.hypothesis: If we publish 12 节气-anchored market-list carousels on 小红书 over 6 weeks and route every commenter to a personal WeChat, then we will collect 150+ WeChat adds and convert 10+ of them to a paid ¥39 seasonal pack within 45 days.
entry_points.expected_upside: 10-30 paying users x ¥39 = ¥390-¥1,170 (~USD 55-165) in the first cycle. Real upside is the WeChat list: at a 5-8% list-to-paid rate on a warm private-domain list, 1,000 WeChat contacts supports ¥6,400-¥15,900/yr at the ¥128 annual pass.
entry_points.risk: 小红书 organic reach for new accounts has tightened materially and off-platform diversion is exactly what the platform suppresses - posts get 限流, the funnel never fills, and the founder burns 12 weeks producing content for a channel that will not let them own the audience.

estimated_cost.notes: Photography and cooking time dominate. Zero cash. The real cost is that this is the most time-expensive of the three and produces the least durable asset.

evidence_needed: Do 10 free market-list posts produce any WeChat adds at all? Fewer than 20 adds from 10 posts means the hook is wrong, not the channel.
Of the first 100 WeChat adds, does anyone reply to a soft ¥39 offer? A 0% reply rate at ¥39 kills the consumer-paid thesis and forces a pivot to B2B/commerce.
Whether the account gets 限流 for CTA-to-WeChat language - test with and without an explicit CTA.
supporting_evidence: no evidence: no search-volume or engagement data found for 节气食谱 on 小红书 specifically. The cultural salience of 二十四节气 is well documented; its commercial pull as a content hook is not.
entry_points.revenue_path: Free 节气 carousel on 小红书 -> comment 食单 -> personal WeChat add -> free full PDF delivered in WeChat -> 3 weeks of free value in a 微信群 -> ¥39 current-season pack sold on 小报童 with a ¥19 早鸟 code for the first 20 -> repeat buyers upgraded to the ¥128 annual pass at the next 节气 turn.

entry_points.name: 小报童 paid column - 二十四节气 一周食单 annual pass
entry_points.target_audience: Chinese knowledge-payment buyers who have already bought at least one paid column or 知识星球 - a demonstrably payment-habituated cohort - who cook for a family and want the weekly what-to-buy, what-to-cook decision made for them. Selected for by prior purchase, which is the only audience characteristic that predicts a second purchase.
entry_points.problem: They will happily pay to stop making the same low-value decision 52 times a year. They are not buying recipes (free everywhere) - they are buying a scheduled, opinionated, finite weekly decision delivered on a calendar they already believe in.
entry_points.hook: 《二十四节气·菜市场食单》第一期 白露：这一周买什么、怎么做、花多少钱，我替你想好了
entry_points.content_format: One 1,200-1,800 word paid post per 节气 (every ~15 days), fixed structure: 本节气该买的5样 / 一周7天食单表 / 3道详解菜 / 采购清单与预算. Plus one free public post per 节气 as the sample.
entry_points.recommended_channel: 小报童 (with a 微信公众号 opened in parallel so 付费阅读 unlocks at the 3-month mark)
entry_points.cta: 订阅《二十四节气·菜市场食单》全年 ¥128，前 20 名 ¥69 —— 一年 24 期，每期都在节气当天送到你微信
entry_points.hypothesis: If we launch a ¥39 single-season 小报童 column to a warm WeChat list and existing 知识付费 communities, then we get 10 paying strangers within 30 days and can measure whether at least 40% of them renew into the ¥128 annual pass at the next season boundary.
entry_points.expected_upside: First cycle 10-50 subs x ¥39 = ¥390-¥1,950 net of the 15% platform fee. A column reaching 300 annual subs at ¥128 is ~¥38,400/yr gross (~USD 5,300) - modest, but real recurring revenue with near-zero COGS, and it validates LTV before any spend on acquisition.
entry_points.risk: Nobody pays. Chinese consumers demonstrably do not pay for recipes - 下厨房 built the category and still had to monetize through commerce, B2B and courses rather than consumer subscription. If the product reads as recipes rather than as a decision made for you on a schedule, price sensitivity is near-total and conversion is zero at any price above ¥0.

estimated_cost.notes: 小报童 takes 15% of revenue; 个税 and WeChat Pay fees are charged separately on top. No business license, no ICP备案, no upfront cash. Writing time only.

evidence_needed: Does anyone pay ¥39 for the first pack? Ten strangers is the whole test. Fewer than three means the model is wrong, not the copy.
Do first-pack buyers renew at the next season boundary? Renewal, not first purchase, decides whether to keep going.
What price does the market bear - run ¥19 / ¥39 / ¥69 against three cohorts before settling.
Whether the founder can sustain 24 issues a year. A missed 节气 is a visible broken promise in a calendar-shaped product.
supporting_evidence: no evidence: doc.zsxq.com is blocked from this environment, so 知识星球 exact fees could not be verified against 小报童. The 800-subscriptions-in-7-days case study is a self-reported creator account on a marketing site, not audited data - treat as anecdote.
entry_points.revenue_path: Free sample post (public) -> shared into 知识付费 / 美食 WeChat groups and posted to 即刻/知乎 -> 小报童 checkout in WeChat, one tap, WeChat Pay -> ¥39 season pack -> renewal offer at the season boundary -> ¥128 annual pass -> the annual pass is the first asset with a measurable LTV to compare against CAC.

entry_points.name: Diaspora price-arbitrage test - bilingual seasonal newsletter to overseas Chinese
entry_points.target_audience: Overseas Chinese (North America, Australia, UK) aged 28-50 who cook Chinese food at home, earn in USD/CAD/AUD, and already pay for content at Western price points. Willingness-to-pay signal: USD 5/mo for a cooking newsletter and USD 40/yr for NYT Cooking are unremarkable there - roughly 5-8x the mainland price ceiling for identical content.
entry_points.problem: They want to eat the way their family ate at 白露 or 冬至, but the Western supermarket produce calendar does not map onto the 节气 calendar, the ingredient names do not translate, and the substitutions are guesswork. Nobody is writing this for them.
entry_points.hook: What My Grandmother Would Cook This Week - and What to Buy Instead When Your Supermarket Does Not Sell It
entry_points.content_format: Weekly bilingual email, 700-1,000 words: the current 节气, what it traditionally calls for, exact Western-supermarket substitutions with brand/aisle specificity, one full recipe. Every issue free for the first 12 weeks.
entry_points.recommended_channel: Substack (email - the only owned, portable, platform-risk-free asset of the three)
entry_points.cta: Subscribe free - and get the Chinese Seasonal Pantry and Market Guide (USD 19) if you want the whole year mapped out
entry_points.hypothesis: If we publish 12 weekly bilingual seasonal issues to overseas Chinese cooks via Substack and Xiaohongshu overseas audience, then we build a 500+ email list and sell 15+ copies of a USD 19 one-off guide within 90 days - testing whether the same content earns 5x more per buyer outside the mainland.
entry_points.expected_upside: 15-40 x USD 19 = USD 285-760 in the first cycle. The strategic upside is far larger: if this converts, the entire content library re-prices at USD 29-39/yr instead of ¥128/yr, roughly tripling revenue per user for zero extra production cost. This is the single highest-leverage experiment in the set.
entry_points.risk: The payment rail. Substack pays out through Stripe, and Stripe explicitly does not serve mainland-China-based users - if the founder cannot produce a Stripe-eligible entity or bank account, the paid tier is simply unavailable and this becomes an unmonetizable list. Fallback rails (Gumroad or Lemon Squeezy with a PayPal payout, or charging diaspora buyers in RMB via WeChat Pay, which many still hold) must be confirmed BEFORE writing issue one. Secondary risk: writing convincingly for a Western-supermarket context requires having actually shopped in one.

estimated_cost.notes: Substack is free until you charge; Gumroad and Lemon Squeezy take a per-sale cut with no upfront fee. Budget 2-3 hours purely to verify which rail can actually pay this founder - that verification is worth more than any content produced this quarter.

evidence_needed: THE BLOCKER: can this founder legally receive USD today, and through which rail? Confirm before anything else.
Do overseas Chinese cooks open a bilingual seasonal email? Measure open rate, not subscriber count.
Does the USD 19 guide sell to anyone who is not a friend? One stranger sale at USD 19 is worth more information than 100 mainland ¥39 sales.
Whether the founder has genuine Western-supermarket knowledge or is guessing - readers detect the difference immediately.
supporting_evidence: no evidence: no data found on paying-subscriber counts or conversion rates for Chinese-language food newsletters aimed at the diaspora. The price-arbitrage thesis rests on general Western price norms, not on any observed instance of this specific product working.
entry_points.revenue_path: Free weekly bilingual issue -> shared in overseas WeChat groups and posted to Xiaohongshu with an overseas-supermarket angle -> email list (owned, portable) -> USD 19 one-off Pantry and Market Guide via Gumroad/Lemon Squeezy -> buyers upgraded to a USD 29-39/yr seasonal pass once the rail and the renewal behaviour are both proven.

what_i_would_not_do: Build an app, a paywall, or a subscription billing system before ten strangers have paid ¥39 for a PDF. Recipe apps are where founder-months go to die; the content itself is infinitely free and low-priced apps convert worse than high-priced ones.

Register a company, apply for 营业执照, open a WeChat Pay merchant account, or file ICP备案 before there is revenue. 小报童 and 公众号付费阅读 let an individual collect money legally today with none of it. Spending six weeks on paperwork before the first sale is the most common way this product dies.

Chase English-language recipe SEO. The most saturated content market on the internet, dominated by incumbents with a decade of domain authority, and recipe traffic is being actively eaten by AI answers.

Build on grocery or ingredient affiliate revenue. Amazon Associates pays 1% on grocery/Amazon Fresh; a nano-audience produces single-digit dollars, and there is no comparable rail for a mainland creator.

Take brand sponsorship or 商单 as the first revenue model. It requires follower count (a banned metric here), makes the founder an employee of an advertiser rather than an owner of an audience, and teaches nothing about whether anyone will pay for the product.

Give away a generous free newsletter for six months with a plan to monetize later. The audience trained to consume for free is the audience that churns at the paywall. Put a price on something in week three, even if it is ¥19.

Sell into Western CSA farms as the opening move. Their software already generates recipes from the weekly harvest list, they pay only USD 80-200/mo for their whole stack, and the sales cycle is a season long.
Optimize for 小红书 follower count. The only number that matters on 小红书 is WeChat adds, and the only number that matters in WeChat is paid conversions.
biggest_unknown: The founder legal residence and what payment rail they can actually collect on today - mainland-resident-with-no-entity versus overseas-or-incorporated inverts the entire recommended sequence, changes the price point by roughly 5x, and decides whether entry point C3 is the highest-leverage experiment in the set or literally impossible to execute. Two hours of verification here is worth more than two weeks of content.
